name: Santiniketan
shortDescription: The educational and artistic community founded by the Tagore family, known for its distinctive campus architecture.
description: Santiniketan began as a meditation retreat and grew into a school and university, Visva-Bharati, founded by Rabindranath Tagore. It is known for its open-air teaching and its blending of Indian and other cultural traditions.
historicalBackground: In 1863 Maharshi Debendranath Tagore, the father of Rabindranath Tagore, established an ashram on land in Birbhum, in the countryside of West Bengal. It was meant as a place for prayer and meditation, free from images, where people of any religion could come. The Upasana Griha, a glass-walled prayer hall, was built in 1891.

In 1901 Rabindranath Tagore started an experimental school here, with classes held under trees. He wished to create an education that was close to nature and encouraged creativity, in contrast with the rote learning of colonial schools. After he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the school drew greater attention.

Visva-Bharati was established in 1921 as an international university, bringing together learning from India and the world. It became a central university in 1951. Its departments include Kala Bhavana (art), Sangit Bhavana (music) and Cheena Bhavana (Chinese studies).

The painters Nandalal Bose, Benode Behari Mukherjee and Ramkinkar Baij taught here and developed what is sometimes called the Bengal School's later phase and early modernism. Their murals and sculptures decorate the campus. The architecture, including Uttarayan complex and the Mud House, uses local materials, mud and thatch alongside modern forms.

Santiniketan became a symbol of Tagore's cultural vision, and a pan-Asian meeting place. It was inscribed by UNESCO in 2023. It remains an active educational campus, so conservation must balance heritage, development and community use.
culturalSignificance: It represents a unique educational and cultural experiment in modern India.
It shows an Indian modernism that combines tradition and international ideas.
It is a living campus with ongoing cultural festivals, such as the Poush Mela and Basanta Utsav.

currentCondition.note: A living university campus; heritage buildings are in use, with development pressure around them.

name: Moidams - the Mound-Burial System of the Ahom Dynasty
shortDescription: Earthen burial mounds of the Ahom kings and nobles, in the royal necropolis of Charaideo.
description: The moidams are dome-shaped mounds covering burial chambers of Ahom rulers and aristocrats. Charaideo, the first Ahom capital, has the largest and most sacred of these.
historicalBackground: The Ahoms were a Tai-speaking people who entered the Brahmaputra valley under their leader Sukaphaa in the early 13th century (traditionally 1228) and founded a kingdom with its first capital at Charaideo. They ruled Assam for almost 600 years until the British annexation in 1826, and are known for successfully resisting Mughal expansion.

Charaideo remained a sacred centre even after the capital moved. The Ahoms buried their kings and members of the royal family in moidams, a practice from their Tai heritage. The body was placed in a vaulted chamber with personal items, and according to old practice, with attendants and servants. A mound of earth was heaped on top and covered with grass or trees.

Over time the moidams grew larger and were built of brick, stone and earth, with an arched passage, an octagonal boundary wall and a pavilion on top (the chow chali). Some mounds are over 15 m high. About 90 royal moidams survive at Charaideo, together with other burial grounds in the area.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, as Hinduism became more important at the Ahom court, rulers began to prefer cremation, and burial of the ashes at Charaideo. Some moidams were reportedly looted during invasions, including by the forces of the Mughal general Mir Jumla in 1662-63, according to the chronicles.

The moidams are still considered sacred, and rituals are performed there. They are also part of the identity of the Assamese people. In July 2024 they were inscribed by UNESCO, the first cultural site from North-East India to be added to the list.
culturalSignificance: It shows a distinct mound-burial tradition of the Ahom dynasty.
It represents the history of the Tai-Ahom people in Assam.
It is a sacred site for the community.

currentCondition.note: Many mounds survive in grassy hills; some are damaged by erosion, vegetation and past looting.

name: Maratha Military Landscapes of India
location: Twelve forts across Maharashtra and Gingee in Tamil Nadu
shortDescription: A network of twelve 17th-19th century forts that expressed Maratha military strategy.
description: The group includes the forts of Salher, Shivneri, Lohgad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg and Gingee. They use hills, forests, coasts and islands for defence.
historicalBackground: The Maratha state was founded by Shivaji Bhonsle (1630-1680), who built a kingdom in the Sahyadri hills and the Konkan coast against the Adil Shahi, Mughal and Siddi powers. He was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. His strategies emphasised guerrilla warfare, fast movement and a network of forts.

The forts fall into types. Hill forts such as Salher, Rajgad, Raigad, Pratapgad and Shivneri use the steep Sahyadri ranges. Plateau forts, such as Panhala, were large bases. Coastal and island forts, such as Sindhudurg, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg and Khanderi, protected the Konkan coast and supported a navy. Gingee in Tamil Nadu, taken by Maratha forces in 1677, is a hill fortress in the south.

Raigad served as the capital, and houses the remains of the royal court and palace. Shivaji was buried there after his death in 1680. Sindhudurg, built from 1664 on an island off Malvan, has thick walls and was used to protect the sea route. Pratapgad is famous as the setting of Shivaji's encounter with the Bijapur general Afzal Khan in 1659.

The Marathas continued to use and extend the forts under later leaders and the Peshwas in the 18th century. After the Anglo-Maratha wars, the British took control of many in the early 19th century and in some cases dismantled their defences.

In July 2025 the group was inscribed by UNESCO as India's 44th World Heritage Site. The forts are maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India and state agencies, and are important in local history and tourism.
culturalSignificance: It shows a strategic use of landscape in military architecture.
It is an important part of the identity and history of Maharashtra.
It represents the Maratha empire's land and sea defence.

currentCondition.note: Condition varies by fort; some are well preserved while others are partly ruined.

architecturalStyle: Maratha military architecture (hill, plateau, coastal and island forts)

name: Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath
shortDescription: The site of the Buddha's first sermon, with stupas, monastery ruins and the Ashokan pillar.
description: Sarnath is where, according to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha gave his first teaching after enlightenment. The site has the Dhamek Stupa, remains of monasteries and temples, and the base of an Ashokan pillar.
historicalBackground: After his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, the Buddha is said to have travelled to the Deer Park at Isipatana (modern Sarnath), near Varanasi, and delivered his first sermon, the Dhammachakkappavattana Sutta, to five ascetics. This event, the 'turning of the wheel of dharma', marks the beginning of the Buddhist community (sangha).

In the 3rd century BCE the Mauryan emperor Ashoka built monuments at Sarnath, including a polished sandstone pillar surmounted by a lion capital with four lions facing outwards. The capital is now in the Sarnath Museum, and was adopted as India's national emblem in 1950.

Over later centuries Sarnath developed into a large monastic centre. The Dhamek Stupa, about 33 m high, was built in the Gupta period (around the 5th-6th century CE) over an earlier structure. The Dharmarajika stupa and the Mulagandha Kuti vihara are other important structures. In the Gupta period Sarnath was also known for a school of Buddha sculpture, whose seated Buddha in teaching posture is celebrated. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described a thriving community in the 7th century.

In the 12th century, Queen Kumaradevi of the Gahadavala dynasty built a large monastery, and the site was in use until it was attacked and burned around 1194. Sarnath fell into ruin, and bricks were removed from the ruins for building. In 1794 workers of Jagat Singh, minister to the Raja of Benares, dismantled the Dharmarajika stupa for bricks and found a relic casket.

Systematic study started with Alexander Cunningham in 1835-36, followed by excavations led by F. O. Oertel (1904-05), John Marshall and Daya Ram Sahni. These revealed monasteries, stupas and sculptures. In July 2026 Sarnath was inscribed by the World Heritage Committee as India's 45th World Heritage Site, so its UNESCO record and dossier are very recent and worth checking again when you finalise the project.
culturalSignificance: It is one of the four principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites.
It is the source of the lion capital used as India's national emblem.
It documents the development of Buddhist art and monasteries from the Mauryan period to the 12th century.

currentCondition.note: An archaeological site with the Dhamek Stupa still standing and other monuments in ruins.
